newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Agendas vary for Singapore world trade talks.
newsitem.headline: Agendas vary for Singapore world trade talks.

text.p: Trading nations have varying agendas for this week's first-ever Ministerial Conference of the World Trade Organisation in Singapore.
The following is a look at what the big powers and key groups from the developed and developing world in the 125-member body would like to see happen at the week-long gathering.
THE UNITED STATES

The United States wants primarily an ITA, a global agreement to end all tariffs on information technology products, computer software and hardware, semiconductors and telecommunications equipment by the year 2000.
"That is the main thing that can demonstrate that the WTO can continuously open markets and increase the rule of law in trade," Deputy U.S. Trade Representative Jeffrey Lang said recently.

Washington also wants the ministers to talk about the relationship between core labour standards and trade to show U.S. workers -- fearful that free trade means less jobs for them -- that the WTO is alive to their concerns.

Another item on the U.S. shopping list is agreement by developing countries to join a WTO government procurement code, under which they would pledge more transparency in awarding official contracts. At present, U.S. officials say, this area is riddled with corruption.
THE EUROPEAN UNION

The European Union wants an accord to start talks at the WTO on national competition policies, with the aim of eventual elimination of cartels and price-fixing agreements between private companies that keep foreign firms out of local markets.

EU Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan would like to see agreement on preparing another global round of trade negotiations to start at the end of the century. But he has won little support, even among EU member states.
Some EU members -- especially France -- agree with the United States that talks on the labour link should begin in the WTO. Others -- Britain, Germany and Spain -- are opposed.
The EU also says it wants an ITA, but prefers a longer time-frame for ending all tariffs.
JAPAN

Japan, together with Canada, is leading a push -- backed by the EU but not by the United States -- for starting talks in the WTO on global rules for the treatment of foreign investment, aimed at ensuring that outside firms get similar treatment to national investors in all member countries.
Tokyo also wants an ITA and is more or less in agreement with the United States on the time-frame. But it is not backing Washington on the labour issue.

Japan agrees there should be talks on competition policy, but -- with South Korea and Latin American countries -- argues this should include anti-dumping, or special tariffs. The EU and the United States, the main practitioners of anti-dumping measures, refuse to accept the link.
EMERGING ASIAN ECONOMIES
Emerging Asian economies want a focus in Singapore on how agreements in the 1986-93 Uruguay Round on cutting tariffs and reducing other barriers to trade are being implemented.

They want the United States and European Union to agree to open up their markets for textile and clothing much more quickly than the 10-year timetable to which the two big powers committed themselves in the Round's Final Act, signed in Marrakesh in April 1994. Although they accept the two powers are observing the letter of the agreement, they say they are violating its spirit.

With India, Malaysia and Indonesia the most vocal, they reject any discussion of "new issues" like labour, investment and competition at this stage, arguing there is enough already on the WTO plate. And they say they cannot consider joining the procurement code.
LATIN AMERICAN COUNTRIES

Latin American countries have no overall agenda for Singapore and take a generally flexible line on the "new issues", saying that if there is consensus to start discussion on them they will not object.
But like the Asians, they would prefer to concentrate on implementation of the Marrakesh accords.

However Argentina, backed by fellow members of the Mercosur grouping Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay, wants the ministers in Singapore to agree on preparations for new talks due to start by the year 2000 on lowering further barriers to agricultural trade. This is being resisted by the EU, Japan and South Korea, whose policy-makers are under fierce pressure from farmers who say they gave away too much in the Uruguay Round.
AFRICAN STATES

African states, many of whom are among the 48 around the world designated by the United Nations as the planet's least-developed countries or LDCs, want the ministers to recognise in concrete terms that they are a special case and stand to be the losers from liberalisation of international trade.

They hope for approval of a plan of action promoted by WTO Director-General Renato Ruggiero to phase out tariffs and other barriers to their products in developed and more advanced developing countries.

Tanzania has emerged as a spokesman at the WTO for this group as well as other sub-Saharan African countries, and has vocally backed the Asians in rejecting introduction of "new issues" on to the agenda.
